summary: For ages 5–7, build the big picture that animals live all over the world — on land, in water, and in the air — on every continent including icy Antarctica, and that each kind is found where it fits. Anchor on a world map/globe, start from the familiar (garden, farm, park) and widen outward to extreme places (deep ocean, polar ice, hot desert), so the recurring 'even here?!' reveal does the conceptual work. Seed 'suited to its place' lightly with one obvious pairing, without teaching the adaptation mechanism (a later topic). Picture-exploration is the main scaffold; a drag-to-sort activity adds active commitment, and a brief sort/match can check recall.
misconceptions: Believing animals only live where the child has seen them (the garden, the zoo, the farm) — missing that animals inhabit the whole planet, including places the child will never visit.
Thinking nowhere as harsh as Antarctica, the deep sea or the desert could have animals — 'nothing lives there'.
Using 'animal' to mean only furry mammals or pets, excluding fish, birds, insects and minibeasts from the category.
Assuming an animal could live just anywhere — not yet noticing that a fish needs water or a polar bear needs cold; the 'suited to its place' idea has to be pointed out.
Confusing where an animal is kept (a zoo, a farm) with where its kind naturally lives in the world.

activities.title: Populate the world map — the 'even here?!' explorer
steps: Start on a big world map or globe at something familiar to the child (a garden, a farm, a park) and name the animals that live there.
Travel outward together — country, ocean, poles, desert — placing or revealing animals on each continent and realm as you go.

At each extreme place, pause and predict before revealing: 'Do you think ANYTHING lives on the freezing white ice of Antarctica?' Then reveal penguins and seals; on the empty-looking desert reveal a camel and a scorpion; in the dark deep sea reveal strange glowing fish.

Re-sort the same animals three ways — land, water, air — talking about where each one mostly lives or moves. Some animals use more than one, for example penguins and seals swim in the sea but also come out onto land and ice, and many birds fly but also walk on land.
For any animal, say its name and share one short wonder-fact.
By the end, check the child can point to several continents that have animals and say aloud that animals live on land, in the water, and in the air.
activities.insight: Animals fill the whole planet — not only where the child has personally been — and they can be grouped by the broad realms land, water and air.

activities.title: Sort the animals to where they live
steps: Take a set of animal pictures and sort each one onto a world map or into three bins labelled land, water and air.
Say out loud where each animal belongs before placing it.
Try a deliberate mismatch — put a fish on the desert — and talk about what would go wrong there.
Aim to put at least one animal on every continent, so no continent is left empty.
activities.insight: Committing to a placement, and noticing when a placement 'can't be right', gives a first gentle taste that an animal fits its own kind of place.

activities.title: First taste of 'suited to its place'
steps: Look at one vivid, obvious pairing — a thick-furred animal in the cold, or an animal with webbed feet in water — and notice how the animal 'fits' where it lives.
Consider a swap question: 'Could a polar bear live happily in a hot, sandy desert? Could a camel live happily on the icy snow of Antarctica?' Tell why or why not for each.
Line up the animal's features against the conditions — thick warm fur is great in ice but would make the animal far too hot in the desert.
Name an animal that lives somewhere with no people at all.
activities.insight: Animals live all over the world, but each one lives where its body fits the conditions; you cannot simply swap an animal into any place.

checkQuestion: Could a polar bear live happily in a hot, sandy desert? And could a camel live happily out on the icy snow of Antarctica? Tell me why or why not for each one.
checkAnswer: No to both. Each animal is suited to its own home. The polar bear's thick fur and blubber would make it far too hot in the desert; the camel is built for heat and dryness, not freezing ice. Animals live all over the world, but each one lives where its body fits the conditions.
